title: Vectors & Motion in Two Dimensions
summary: Vectors have magnitude and direction; they add by components. In two dimensions, motion separates into independent $x$ and $y$ parts — the key to projectile motion, where horizontal velocity is constant and vertical motion is free fall.

vector.plain: A quantity with magnitude and direction.
vector.in_class: Add by components, not by simple sums.

components.plain: A vector's projections onto the axes.

resultant.plain: The vector sum of several vectors.

projectile motion.in_class: Constant horizontal velocity; vertical free fall.

independence of motion.plain: $x$ and $y$ motions don't affect each other.
independence of motion.in_class: Solve them separately, linked only by time.

concept_sections.heading: Vector components
concept_sections.explanation: Break a vector into $A_x=A\cos\theta$ and $A_y=A\sin\theta$. Components add like ordinary numbers, which makes vector addition manageable.

concept_sections.heading: Adding vectors
concept_sections.explanation: The resultant is found by summing components, then converting back to magnitude and direction. Graphically it's the tip-to-tail sum.

concept_sections.heading: Independence of 2D motion
concept_sections.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent, connected only through the shared time. Analyze each with 1D kinematics.
math_steps: Use the common time to link them.

concept_sections.heading: Projectile motion
concept_sections.explanation: With gravity only, horizontal velocity stays constant and vertical motion is free fall. The path is a parabola.
math_steps: Combine for time of flight, range, height.

concept_sections.heading: Range and maximum height
concept_sections.explanation: Time of flight comes from the vertical motion; range is horizontal velocity times that time; max height occurs when $v_y=0$.

real_world_examples.title: A kicked football
real_world_examples.scenario: A ball launched at an angle.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Its range and hang time come from splitting the launch velocity into components.

real_world_examples.title: A boat crossing a river
real_world_examples.scenario: A boat aims across a current.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The boat's velocity and the current add as vectors to give the real path.

real_world_examples.title: Water from a hose
real_world_examples.scenario: A stream arcs to the ground.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The parabolic trajectory follows from independent horizontal and vertical motion.
